course_title: Studies in Africana Literature and Culture
description: This course introduces students to works by female authors of African descent in the Americas, Europe and Africa. The aim is for students to understand social, political and historical issues and concerns that have traditionally influenced Black women writers writing from Africa, the United States and the Caribbean. In our readings of texts, discussions, and group works, we will oscillate between these Course Syllabus regions as we consider the impact of political experiences of gender inequalities, colonialism, anti colonial resistance, nationalism, and decolonization as contexts for literary productions. We will begin with the image of Africa as the “Dark Continent” by considering the origins of this formation and the harm it has produced; we will then move on to consider ways that Black women writers, from Africa and the diaspora, contest this image by providing alternatives representations of race, cultural and national identity, gender, and the impact of capitalist globalization.

course_title: Followership: The Other Side of Leadership
description: There is no leadership without followership. Every leader is a follower first. Every system rises or falls on the quality of followership within it. And yet, followership is rarely studied with seriousness, depth, or respect. This course exists to change that. This class treats followership as: • A legitimate and necessary field of study • A moral and ethical practice • A source of power, voice, courage, and responsibility • A daily lived experience, not a secondary role Students will be challenged to examine assumptions, question norms, engage with complexity, and develop a thoughtful, personal stance on what it means to follow well.

Explores the paleoecological context in which past humans interacted with the natural environment encompassing plants, animals and landscape. Introduces students to theories and methods relevant to studying past human-environment interactions. Outlines types of environmental data that survive in the archaeological record (geological, botanical, faunal, chemical), recovery and analytical methods, absolute chronology, and inferences made based on these data. Defines and discusses key concepts, such as health, illness, and disease, in relation to various social, environmental, political, and evolutionary contexts. Engages with contemporary and emerging issues in health and healthcare, emphasizing the comparative analysis of global medical systems. Compares and contrasts biomedicine with other ethnomedical systems to evaluate its role within diverse cultural contexts. Develops a greater understanding of the breadth of variation in the human condition and the power of culture to shape individual experience. description:

contemporary issues in science - current questions, discoveries, and challenges that shape our 
understanding of the environment. Topics may include climate change, energy systems, plastics and 
pollution, agriculture, water and food safety, biodiversity, environmental health, and chemicals and drugs 
(including vaccines). Students will learn to evaluate scientific claims and critically analyze how science is 
presented in the news, on television, and on social media.

course_title: The Science and Politics of Climate Change
description: This course investigates the (pseudo-)scientific debate over Global Warming, and available technological options and policies to address it. It considers climate science history, facts, denialism, and the understanding and perceptions of the public in light of the developing climate situation (particularly climate change impacts) and the current political stances. It explores our options for responding to climate change and how to evaluate them, presenting an overview of the (technological) options to transition to a climate-neutral society considering the necessary navigation of a gridlocked political debate in the US. This course is designed for upper-level undergraduate students.

Examination of the science of climate change; past and present causes of global-scale climate change; basis for projections of future climate change and its potential impacts; existing and proposed policy responses; critical evaluation of scientific information.

course_title: Content-Area Instruction for Bilingual Programs/ Instrucción de materias académicas básicas en programas bilingües
description: This course addresses research-based pedagogy for emergent bilingual/English learner students. We will explore through our readings, your field observations, and our discussions, the theories, methodologies, and approaches for designing and delivering literacy infused STEM-based inquiry lessons across content areas (transdisciplinary). We will also examine L1 (home language) and L2 (target language [English]) as languages of instruction in the content areas and how to incorporate creative problem-solving and critical thinking into STEM-based lessons.

course_title: Bilingual Assessment and Monitoring for Bilingual Programs (Evaluación y monitoreo de programas educativos bilingües)
description: This course, which is conducted in Spanish, introduces you to bilingual assessment, assessment of English learners, and factors that influence the validity of assessment results and their interpretation. We will also explore assessment and its relationship to language policy through monitoring of bilingual education programs by government, state, and local education agencies. Through our readings, your field observations, and our class discussions we will probe the relationship of assessment to lesson design, effective pedagogy, teacher-based practices, and critical thinking.

course_title: Special Topics in Extinction Risk Assessment
description: This course aims to train advanced undergraduate and graduate students to prepare scientifically rigorous extinction risk assessments under the categories and criteria approved by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN). The IUCN is the world’s leading authority on the conservation status of species. Students will learn to interpret and apply the IUCN Red List Categories and Criteria, compile supporting information, create distribution maps and manage data. They will work individually and in teams to prepare assessments of species, mirroring the process used by the IUCN Red List species specialist groups. Texas A&M participates in the IUCN Red List Partnership, and students will have opportunities to interact with species’ specialists.

The focus will be on using cultural models to facilitate effective collaboration in international settings, involving students, faculty, and industry partners in the design thinking process. Key components of the course include active participation in teams (with Greek students) working on real-world projects and collaboration with project sponsors and stakeholders. The course will take place in Thessaloniki and Athens, Greece, and consist of 45 contact hours. This course is a requirement for obtaining the Texas A&M International Engineering Certificate.

This course examines how and why societies make decisions about environmental issues. We will explore major conceptual frameworks for governing human-environment interactions, including regulatory, market-based, and community-based governance. Building on these and other frameworks, we will develop an analytical toolset to describe and analyze environmental decision-making in terms of policy design, institutional and political power relations, values and knowledge systems, scalar characteristics, and effectiveness. In-class activities will put this toolset to work by unpacking environmental governance case studies from various contexts. The course will culminate in a final research project centered on proposing solutions to a real-world environmental governance challenge

course_title: Inter-American Affairs: US Interventions in Latin America and Beyond
description: This course examines the dynamics of contemporary Inter-American political relations, with an emphasis on policy and security issues affecting the United States, Canada, the Caribbean, and Latin America. It explores the modern history of the United States through the lens of interventions, spanning from the Marine assault on Tripoli in 1805 to the military intervention in Libya in 2011. Focusing on invasions, coups, and other interventions, this course tries to understand the motives behind each action, analyze the strategies used, and determine the impacts on both American history and the world in the longer term. Through the study of each intervention, we will aim to not only to understand the local events that led to the incidents, but also to see the patterns and themes that show the driving forces of American interventionism. Beginning with an exploration of the ideological roots of American interventionism, we trace its evolution across key periods, including the Spanish-American War, the era of gunboat diplomacy, and the clandestine interventions of the Cold War era. We will then explore the modern age of invasions, marked by conflicts in Afghanistan and Iraq. As we conclude, we encounter the pressing question of future interventions, recognizing the centrality of this issue in American foreign policy debates and the importance of learning from the past to inform contemporary decision-making.

Develop theoretical knowledge of the discipline including the history of how the discipline developed and its role in the broader forensic sciences and international, federal, and state levels. Apply proper anatomical terminology, taphonomy, and comparative morphological methods to discuss and describe skeletal trauma, pathologies, and anomalies. Apply and practice methods used to create a "biological profile" for an individual by estimating sex, age, stature, and ancestry. Explore scene recovery methods and how skeletal analysis is applied in a variety of contexts, including routine casework, large-scale natural disasters, war casualties, and human rights investigations. Critically discuss and analyze forensic methods by addressing the practical, ethical, and contested issues/topics facing contemporary forensic anthropologists.

Investigates anthropology as the holistic and relativistic study of humankind, exploring human life across diverse cultures, time periods, and geographical locations. Examines the discipline through its four major subfields: archaeology (the study of material culture and the past), biological anthropology (the study of Page 1 of 12 Course Syllabus human evolution and variation), sociocultural anthropology (the study of cultural systems and social organization), and linguistic anthropology (the study of language construction and symbolism). Applies fundamental concepts, including the scientific method and evolutionary theory, to complex human experiences. Develops abilities in critical thinking, analysis of empirical data, and effective communication, engaging with culturally diverse and sometimes controversial subjects. Analyzes the discipline’s relationship with society and its impact on global communities over time.

Exploration of the contemporary and historical cultures of the Middle East region; investigation of intercultural connections between the Middle East and the rest of the globe; emphasis on cultural traditions, religious communities, societal change, social movements, migration, and diaspora.

course_title: Cultural and Ethical Considerations for Global Practice
description: ARCH 458 will introduce you to the contextual peculiarities of different cultures and places. Architecture, as a place-making activity, is a process requiring an understanding of the significance of space and time. This significance is the result of cultural practices. By cultural practices are meant social activities that reproduce social systems, and that provide meaning in everyday life. In this sense understanding each culture’s social and behavioral rituals and systems are seen as the means for, and outcome of, social activities

course_title: Painting and Sculpture in Ancient Architecture
description: ARCH 434 is a course for advanced undergraduates. It is expected that students will already have an understanding of ancient art and architecture and are prepared to engage in rigorous analysis and discussion. Classes will include PowerPoint lectures, discussion of assigned readings, and student presentations. Among the topics to be considered are the development of artistic styles and conventions, iconography and symbolism, art as propaganda, and the power of art and architecture to express identity and beliefs, create historical awareness, and preserve social memory.

Fundamental issues of innovative design processes and creation explored through the creative use of past, present and future materials, tools, and technologies; with an emphasis upon the research of materials, methods, scale, craft and technique as instruments of design, fabrication, and production.

course_title: AREN Heating, Ventilating, and Air Conditioning Design
description: Project-based design course; select and develop the mechanical system for a building, from the programming phase to the design development and working documents; emphasis on the application HVAC principles in the design and analysis of a mechanical system in a real building, including review of building thermal load calculations & energy analysis, HVAC design goals and schematic design, system selection and system design, HVAC design development, HVAC design documents, and energy, environmental, and human comfort considerations in HVAC design.

Application and extension of fundamentals of engineering design, product detail, and design development process, including case studies; emphasis on project management, marketing considerations, manufacturing detailed design specifications, failure modes, applications of codes and standards, selection of design margins, product (component) development guidelines, intellectual property, product liability and ethical responsibility; major architectural engineering design project.

Instruction and practice in the design process applied to an architectural engineering design project; application of establishing customer need, determining requirements in terms of function and performance, developing alternative design concepts, performing trade-off studies among performance, cost and schedule, embodiment and detail design and the iteration of the above steps; major architectural engineering design project.

Introduction to qualitative and quantitative engineering concepts of mechanical systems for buildings for architectural engineers, including HVAC systems, control of indoor air pollutants and fire suppression systems; emphasis on thermal behavior of buildings and building envelopes, human comfort requirements and psychometrics, thermal load calculations, HVAC systems/equipment, design of space air-conditioning and its relationship to architectural design, mechanical systems for indoor air quality and for fire suppression.

Analysis and application of the engineering design process to solve problems associated with the design and operation of building systems, specifically related to HVAC, electrical power and lighting, and structural integrity; communication of solutions to technical problems of building systems, through writing, presentations, and team interactions, typical of architectural engineers in the building industry; emphasis on the engineering design process in architectural engineering, structural systems for buildings, mechanical systems for heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning, electrical lighting for buildings, building fire safety, building acoustics, building codes and standards, interface issues among different building systems, and sustainability aspects of building systems.

Introduction to the broad field and professional practice of architectural engineering, architectural engineering systems, and the role of the architectural engineer; emphasis on professional engineering design services, design and construction processes and documents, building envelope and materials, structural systems, mechanical systems, lighting systems, building systems integration, building codes and standards, fire safety, professional attributes of architectural engineers, and issues of human performance requirements and sustainability at relates to building system design. Prerequisite: Sophomore classification or approval of instructor.

course_title: Student High Impact Experiences in Meteorology Specifically: SEA-Met (Student Experiences Abroad in Meteorology) Barbados: Tropical and Island Meteorology
description: Describe the major meteorological processes affecting weather and climate in the Caribbean Region. • Compare and contrast these processes with those occurring in North America. • Describe the typical climate regimes in a tropical island location, and dependence on island relief. • Identify the major types of easterly waves by satellite and wind analyses. Describe the precipitation characteristics of each, and the underlying dynamical principles. • Compare and contrast operational meteorological structure, tools, and data of the Caribbean Region with those of the U.S National Weather Service. • Participate in group weather briefings. • Set up and operate emergency communications capable of receiving weather information without internet capability (e.g. Ham Radio, HF meteorological facsimile, and/or NAVTEX). (Optional) • Describe the processes which lead to air quality issues of the region. • Demonstrate social, cultural, and global competence: a.) Live and work effectively in a unique global society. b.) Articulate the value of a broad global perspective and cultural understanding. c.) Recognize unique opinions and practices and consider different points of view. • Prepare and deliver oral /and/or poster presentations on the experience to include both scientific and cultural content.
Structure, energy, and motions of the atmosphere; climate; fronts and cyclones; atmospheric stability; clouds and precipitation; severe storms.

Overview of physical, mechanical, fluid dynamical, electrical, optical, and molecular aspects of bioaerosols; bioaerosol generation, sampling and deposition measurements including size distribution, morphology, chemical composition, bioaerosol samplers, sample analysis, dry and wet deposition, and biofilm resuspension; health effects of bioaerosols, antibiotic resistance, ambient sampling in industrial and agricultural fields.

course_title: Biological and Agricultural Engineering Fundamentals I
description: Fundamental engineering concepts related to agricultural systems including the environment (soil, water, and air), plant and animal production systems and processing, and associated machines and facilities; application of techniques for data collection and analysis to problems in biological and agricultural engineering; design of experiments and communication of experimental results. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MEEN 221 or concurrent enrollment

course_title: Seminar (Tree Health in a Changing Climate)
description: This seminar is a capstone course required for BESC majors. The intent of the course is for students to work individually to analyze a single theme related to BESC. The theme will be introduced to the class, followed by students working individually to define and understand the complexities of a specific topic they select from a list provided by the instructor. Students will prepare slideshow/poster presentations and writings on their selected topic. The course will meet weekly for direction by the instructor, but it is expected that most of your research and preparation will take place outside of the classroom. In using this course format, the intended outcome is to allow the student to draw from a wide range of materials and current events to analyze and understand a discrete aspect within the broad area of bioenvironmental sciences.

This course explores modern technologies for detecting environmental contaminants, toxins, and pathogens. We will trace the evolution of diagnostics — from traditional physical and chemical methods to next-generation biotechnology platforms. Students will learn how tools from synthetic biology, soft materials, and device engineering are converging to create living electronic systems capable of rapid, multiplex environmental monitoring. Through case studies, discussions, and examples from current research and industry, students will gain insight into key environmental challenges, innovative detection strategies, and how emerging biotechnologies can strengthen environmental and agricultural health.

Data management, analysis and interpretation specifically for bioenvironmental research purposes; development of skills required to draw conclusions from data, specifically the types of data relevant to studying the interface of biological and environmental processes; exploration of the challenges of bioenvironmental data analysis; exposure to and development of skills in presentations that highlight the challenges of successfully communicating results and conclusions that necessarily rest on interpretation and assumptions. Prerequisite: BESC 201; STAT 201, STAT 302 or STAT 303.

Introduction to environmental sampling and methodology; strategies and analyses of sampling data; overview of current applications of sampling and monitoring in the environmental sciences; emphasis on practical aspects of sampling from air, soil and water; detection and quantification of microbial and chemical unknowns in environmental media. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor

Metabolic pathways of microbes involved in the biodegradation of hazardous materials; ecological requirements for biotreatability of contaminated sites; emphasis on factors affecting microbial growth; strategies for in situ bioaugmentation. Prerequisite: CHEM 222 or CHEM 227.

course_title: Molds and Mushrooms – The Impact of Fungi on Society and the Environment
description: Introduction to fungi and the impact these organisms have on society and the environment; includes life cycles of fungi; classification schemes, pathogens of plants, animals and humans; fungi in food production; toxic fungi and the law; and others.

The application of ethical theory to the use of modern genetics and biochemistry stressing the social implications of genetic engineering, agricultural manipulation and biotechnology. Prerequisites: GENE 302 or GENE 303; BICH 409, BICH 410, or BICH 440. Cross-listed with GENE 420.

Current topics in biomolecules, natural product antibiotics and application in infectious diseases, modern and historical approaches to antibiotic discovery, biomedical glycobiology, glycosylation in diseases and pathobiology.

course_title: Professionalism, Skill Development, Career Exploration, and Ethical Conduct in Biomedical Sciences
description: Exposure to skills and ethical procedures to assist in the professional practice of Biomedical Sciences. Exploration of business and professional concepts from an ethical foundation. Topics cover development of the individual; ethical integrity; interpersonal dynamics; effective communication skills. This course is designed to equip students with essential professional skills and ethical practices that greatly assist students in biomedical science. Beginning with an ethical foundation, this course explores foundational business concepts and communication. The course aims to develop a well-rounded understanding of professional conduct and interpersonal dynamics in the scientific field. Through a blend of theoretical knowledge and practical application, this course prepares students to navigate the complex and evolving landscape of biomedical science with professionalism, ethical integrity, and effective communication.

To explore the concept of One Health; the health of humans, animals, and ecosystems are interconnected and interdependent; the conceptual framework that encompasses human and veterinary medical sciences, agricultural sciences, food safety, public health and epidemiology, environmental health and toxicology, wildlife ecology and conservation, and many related fields of study or research.

Fraud in science, how to recognize it, and how to avoid committing fraud; includes the basis of ethics and plagiarism, negotiation techniques and conflict management, the regulations and ethics covering animal and human experiments, record-keeping, data management and peer review. Prerequisite: BIOL 491, NRSC 491, BICH 491, GENE 491, BIMS 491, CHEM 491, BIOL 351, or BICH 410, or approval of instructor.

Cell biology, molecular biology and biophysics of neurons as it pertains to their fundamental role in the physiological basis of behavior. The course provides students with a foundational understanding of how neurons create, maintain and exploit electrical signals for information coding and transmission. It also introduces principles of electrical and chemical signaling between neurons, and the role of intracellular signaling for signal modulation and synaptic plasticity. Throughout the course students are introduced to a broad range of state-of-the-art molecular tools currently used to study the nervous system, and will learn about the cellular basis for many of the most common neurological disorders affecting humans as well as the strategies and therapies for their treatment.

Analysis of ecosystems at organismal, population, interspecific and community levels.

course_title: Biomedical Monitoring and Diagnostic Sensing Devices
description: Exploration of design, development, and implementation of biomedical diagnostic sensing and monitoring devices for point-of-care deployment in general and for underserved, remote, and under resourced environments; hand-held and wearable sensing and diagnostic modalities and testing platforms with user-focused device design and development.

Examines cancer from an engineering perspective focusing on cancer as a complex interaction of tumor cells, support cells, and immune cells; quantifying and engineering tumor microenvironments; engineering advances in cancer discovery and therapeutic interventions; emphasis on systems integration to address cancer challenges.
Analysis of validation and verification testing for biomedical engineering design, along with manufacturing readiness, market-entry readiness, and post-market engineering activities.
An exploration into democracy, civic engagement, and community leadership with an emphasis on engaging in public service as citizens.

course_title: Bush Undergraduate Success Hub – Civics, Leadership & Democracy
description: An exploration into democracy, civic engagement, and community leadership with an emphasis on engaging in public service as citizens.

Examination of historical trends in philanthropy; participation in grant making process through the lens of a private foundation; engagement with local and national philanthropic leaders; development of personal philanthropic ethic through a grant making simulation. that includes due diligence, writing grants and reaching collective decisions. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
Overview of the major chemical process and related industries including key sectors, history, operating principles, and supply chains; focus on technical, market, sustainability, and safety aspects.

Introduction to interdisciplinary aspects of engineering careers; work engineers perform in their field; engineering practice within realistic constraints, e.g., economic, environmental, ethical, health and safety, and sustainability; engineering design process; effective communication in engineering settings. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisite: Enrollment in the college of engineering.

course_title: Communication and Contemporary Issues: Transnational Media Flows
description: Explores the study of how communication practices construct, contest, circulate and/or suppress contemporary issues. Focus may draw on rhetorical, critical, interpretive and/or empirical approaches to message design, media representation, public discourse, and/or everyday interaction.  Emphasizes analytical reading and case analysis grounded in scholarship. Course focus varies by instructor and term.

Examines propaganda as a strategic form of communication used across political, commercial, and social contexts. Surveys historical and contemporary approaches to influencing mass audiences through language, imagery, narrative, and emotion. Analyzes how persuasive appeals operate in mass media, digital platforms, public relations, advertising, and/or institutional messaging. Considers distinctions between information, persuasion, and manipulation, with attention to credibility, transparency, and ethics. Content may include real-world messages that involve political conflict, sensitive beliefs, or provocative imagery, studied for purposes of critical evaluation.

Examines how new media technologies shape civic participation, public discourse, and/or social change across different political systems. Focus on communication practices in democratic, authoritarian, and/or transitional societies. Considers how digital platforms enable organizing, surveillance, protest, and/or community formation. Emphasizes theory-driven analysis of how online communication intersects with power, governance, and collective life. Engagement with case studies from global and/or local contexts, including instances where media use is celebrated, contested, or restricted. Course content and discussions may draw from different cultural or political contexts, including situations of disagreement or unrest, examined for purposes of understanding communication dynamics.

Strategic communication practice; application of skills including communication research, media writing and advanced media writing, visual media and public speaking, service-learning as not-for-fee consultant to a community organization.

Examine the role of media and its impact on human behavior, emotions and thoughts; topics include mass media, social media and how they influence individual and societal functioning across a range of important psychological topics; e.g., self-image, sexual behavior, mental health, violence. Cross-listed with COMM 316.

Cross-listed with COMM 316.

Communication interventions for personal, organizational, and institutional change; survey of major communication intervention theories in contexts such as voting, purchasing, joining, or adopting; individual-level, interpersonal level, and community-level models of change; application of social science-based models to guide communication intervention strategies effectively.

course_title: Special Topics in Communication, Religion, and the Arts
description: Explores the study of art and religion as forms of communication, with attention to how visual and artistic expression conveys meaning across cultures and traditions. Surveys artistic and media practices in religious and secular contexts, considering how aesthetics mediate religious experience and shape public understanding. Examines the role of art in supporting, questioning, and/or challenging religious and social perspectives. Focus on interpretation and critique, and dialogue of artifacts across diverse traditions, including attention to issues of pluralism, inequality, power, class, and/or representation. Includes engagement with perspectives that may be unfamiliar or challenging, reflecting the diversity of voices in contemporary public life.

description: Explores mass media as a form of communication across cultural, political, and creative contexts. Examines how news media, podcasts, social media, video, television and advertising are used to inform, persuade, critique, and/or tell stories. Analyzes source, audience, message design, and the relationship between medium and purpose. Examines how information, misinformation, and disinformation spreads, developing skills and techniques for assessing credibility and verifying sources. Includes engagement with real-world issues and diverse perspectives may arise through topics connected to politics, culture, ethics, and/or lived experience.

Practicum on leadership skills; leading and managing difficult discussions in a professional setting; mentorship of new students; presentation of difficult discussion topics, demonstrate constructive critique methods. Students enrolled in COSC 322 will attend Monday night lectures (ILCB 112) or as a breakout with the COSC 222 course (ILCB 113) to observe large lectures in preparation for small group discussion. Working with guidance from the small group instructor, students will create discussion plans, practice providing constructive feedback on written and oral communications, demonstrate accountability, and lead discussions in small group settings. Specific topics will cover individual and collective ideas about how values and beliefs are expressed in the construction environment. Discussions will focus on how the field of construction internalizes and thinks about values across cultures and how authority, majorities and privilege affect the built environment. This is an advanced leadership opportunity to emphasize civil discourse to help lower-level students recognize their own positionality and work collaboratively in a multicultural society. (3-0). Credit 3

course_title: Cultural & Social Issues in the Construction Environment
description: Introduction to cultural and social issues in the built environment; exploration of how individual and collective ideas, values and beliefs are expressed in the construction environment; how the field of construction internalizes and thinks about these values across cultures and how authority, majorities and privilege affect the creativity of the built environment; emphasizes civil discourse to help recognize positionality and work collaboratively in a multicultural society.

Integration of nutrition science principles, dietary recommendations, and food and cooking skills to facilitate healthy eating behaviors for health promotion; application to recipe development and modification to meet specific dietary needs and sensory acceptability. Prerequisites: NUTR 301; enrollment in culinary health certificate program; junior or senior classification.

Water quality assessment of natural environmental systems; development and calibration of models to describe fate and transport of contaminants in aquatic systems; application of models to design of water quality control facilities. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in EVEN 301 or CVEN 301. Cross-listed with CVEN 413.

Water quality assessment of natural environmental systems; development and calibration of models to describe fate and transport of contaminants in aquatic systems; application of models to design of water quality control facilities. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in EVEN 301 or CVEN 301. Cross-listed with CVEN 413.

This course is a gateway to solving complex civil engineering challenges involving sustainable flood risk management, water supply, and groundwater. This course builds on fluid mechanics with new theory and applications on hydrology, open channel hydraulics, and pressure conduits. The program will consist of approximately two (2) weeks in The Netherlands! The course format will involve two (2) virtual zoom lectures prior to departure, followed by traditional face-to-face classroom instruction in Amsterdam and Rotterdam, four (4) technical tours, and two (2) cultural excursions. Participants will earn three (3) credits. The Netherlands is considered the Silicon Valley of water resources engineering and sustainable floodplain management. Thus, this course will offer a unique and immersive learning experience unlike any other.

Second course in a two-course sequence for the capstone senior design experience; continuation of work on the senior design project in teams; data collection, analysis, application of data engineering methods and tools and development of recommendations considering design constraints, evaluation of alternative design, and application of relevant standards; engagement in oral presentations and creation of the project report, with relevant feedback provided during the semester. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in DAEN 459

Develop the skills necessary to direct a dance team in secondary education; budgeting, scheduling, and interpersonal relationships; examine the different seasons and their unique needs: football, contest, spring show, summer camps; define injury protocols and discuss return to dance procedures; examine work/life balance; create a professional portfolio specific to directing dance.

Using scientific methods to evaluate the dancer's body; implementation of dance screening process and creation of programs to address specific dance related injuries, imbalances or misalignments; study of current research in dance medicine/science and application of this knowledge to increase longevity of movement.

Introduction to and exploration of the principles of improvisational partnering including touch, trust, weight sharing, and non-verbal communication; experiment with non-codified/free movement in collaboration with peers including concepts of listening, responding, leading, following, pushing, and pulling; understanding principles of safe alignment and lifting; learning about the history of contact improvisation from creation to present day and understanding the social/cultural influences which shape the form.

Dance Appreciation introduces dance including its cultural, social, and artistic aspects. Special emphasis is given to the appreciation and understanding of the role dance plays in various societies and how society influences the development of dance as an art form. This course will explore various artistic dance genres, the cultural influence of dance, and then turn to contemporary culture and current issues in dance.

Overview of ballet and modern dance from the 19th century to the current day with a focus on Europe and the United States. Examines historical events and societal shifts and considers corollaries that may have influenced the evolution of dance; draws parallels to shifts in music and art throughout history. Discussion of impactful choreographers, dancers, musicians, artists, and producers and how their personal philosophies and heritage influenced dance. Course fulfills the required core curriculum components for Language, Philosophy, and Culture (KLPC) and Cultural Discourse (CD) as determined by the university.

course_title: Wildlife Forensic Science: Methods and Applications
description: Introduction to the interdisciplinary field of wildlife forensic science; application of scientific techniques to the investigation of wildlife crimes including poaching, trafficking, and habitat destruction; emphasis on forensic methods such as species identification, DNA analysis, and trace evidence collection; exploration of legal and regulatory frameworks; practical applications of forensic science in conservation and biodiversity protection

Focus on an individual student effort assessing the ecological and human dimensions of biodiversity conservation and nature tourism; exposure to the ecological aspects of managing natural resources, especially wildlife populations and their habitat, as well as the economic, social, and cultural factors affecting biodiversity conservation and nature tourism in a developing country. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with RWFM 400.

Use of prescribed fire to achieve ecosystem management objectives; understanding of how to plan and implement prescribed fires; coursework on fire behavior, fuel properties and the social aspects of prescribed fire and wildfire; how to safely use fire to achieve multiple outcomes including biodiversity conservation, reduced hazardous fire risk, livestock production and timber management

Integration of biophysical, economic and social factors in forest resource analysis, management planning and decision making; applications of interdisciplinary knowledge and multiple-use principles to practical forest management problems.

course_title: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for Resource Management
description: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) approach to solving spatial problems and managing natural resources, including the acquisition, management, manipulation, analysis, and mapping of spatial and non-spatial databases; identification of natural and relevant features from various data sources; integration of relevant technologies and data; extensive use of GIS software to solve real-world problems.

course_title: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for Resource Management
description: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) approach to solving spatial problems and managing natural resources, including the acquisition, management, manipulation, analysis, and mapping of spatial and non-spatial databases; identification of natural and relevant features from various data sources; integration of relevant technologies and data; extensive use of GIS software to solve real-world problems.

Life history and general characteristics of trees; structure and function of forest ecosystems; fundamental principles of forest tree physiology and ecology applied to an analysis of tree growth in relation to environmental factors and present day forest management; global changes and forests. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; introductory courses in ecology and chemistry recommended.

Cycling of the elements like carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus, and their influence on ecosystem functions and the climate system; human impacts on biogeochemistry; global changes that threaten the sustainability of ecosystem services; wildland fire science and fire ecology showing the interrelated nature of the climate system, vegetation and human activities; classic and current scientific literature. Prerequisites: Grade of a C or better in ECCB 205, BIOL 111, or BIOL 112; junior or senior classification or instructor approval.

Life histories of fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals; lecture covers vertebrate groups on a worldwide scale and emphasizes a comparative approach to the study of adaptation to the environment; lecture topics include behavior, reproduction, feeding specializations, evolutionary history, locomotion, hibernation, migration, endangered species, zoogeography and importance to man; laboratory emphasizes the recognition of Texas vertebrates. Designed for both science and non-science majors.

Interpretation of plant morphology for keying and identification of important flowering rangeland plants; vegetative and floral characters for important plant families including toxic compounds affecting domestic livestock. Plant collection required.

course_title: Secondary Education in Ecology and Conservation Biology
description: Introduction to a career as a secondary science teacher and classroom activities in the areas of ecology and conservation biology; presentation of education and certification requirements, exploration of the structure of schools and districts, classroom and professional expectations; overview of departmental and campus resources that will assist with collegiate and career goals.

course_title: Harnessing Solar Energy: Optics, Photovoltaics and Thermal Systems
description: Solar radiation characteristics and measurement; Optical coatings including reflection, transmission, absorption and emissivity; Concentrating optics, tracking and etendue limit; Photovoltaic cells, modules and systems overview. Introduction to solar thermal systems.

The course introduces students to fundamental topics in power and energy systems, including three phase circuits, transformers, and electromechanical system, and prepares them for advanced courses in the area. This contains basic concepts in the conversion of electric energy, either between different types of electric energy, or between electricity and other forms of energy.

course_title: Data Science for Future Decision Makers
description: Integration of fundamental economic concepts, such as the study of how economic incentives impact decision making, with skills and tools from data science that are necessary to work with the vast amounts of data that economic agents generate daily

Personnel Economics. Exploration of the economics of the workplace using the insights of economic models and behavioral economics; focus on incentives and information, motivation of workers through incentive pay, promotion tournaments and threats, design of the hiring process to recruit a talented and diverse workforce, attraction and retention of employees, downsizing.

This course surveys the economics of development. We will study developing countries which constitute most of the world and share some commonalities. We identify the problems that developing countries face and focus on the policies that governments pursue. Since the nature of economic development is complex and broad, we cannot address all issues, and focus selectively on some issues. The course style follows lectures with discussions and plenty of applications to the real world.

Application of economic analysis to education policy; theoretical basis for private and public investment 
in education; returns to education; the importance of school resources, school financing, school choice, 
and accountability.

course_title: Early Childhood and Adolescent Curriculum and Lesson Design
description: Examination of curriculum models used in educational environments designed for young children through adolescents and the organization of the curriculum; investigation of state-adopted curriculum knowledge and skills standards and materials as well as their use and expansion. Prerequisites: EDCI 353; TEFB 371 or concurrent enrollment

course_title: Early Childhood and Adolescent Curriculum and Lesson Design
description: Early childhood through adolescent approaches and instructional materials appropriate for EC through middle school programs; impact of research and theory on child development from gestation to early adolescence on instructional practices. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification

In this course the many ways that individuals think about, and practice conflict management and effective dialogue will be explored. Students will have a chance to learn more about their own negotiating preferences and its impact on self, the workplace, and their careers. Additionally, an aim of this course is to assist learners in the identification and learning of the importance of effective conflict management in the workplace and to develop skills to effectively engage in meaningful conflict using effective modalities for the situation presented. The course requires both intensive involvement in negotiation and mediation simulations/exercises and thoughtful application of theory through class discussion and written analysis. Class materials will reflect a variety of contexts from the workplace, including interpersonal, global, and cross-cultural interactions

By the end of the course, students should be able to: • Describe the field of HRD (to include its primary functions) and provide a historical perspective of its development. Explain the roles and contexts of an HRD professional and discuss challenges faced by the field. • Analyze models and theories of employee behavior and motivation and their application in the workplace and discuss how knowledge, skill, ability, and attitude influence employee behavior. • Explain the role of learning styles and learning strategies in relation to maximizing learning effectiveness. • Identify the basic theories and concepts of organizational development. • Describe how organizational culture is being affected by diversity, and in particular having a greater number of women and minorities in the workplace. • Design, implement, and evaluate HRD programs.

Fundamental design processes, issues and theories relevant to design resolution and the creation of new ideas; creative thought processes from the formation of ideas through incubation to final product and future impact on the physical environment and society.

During the nineteenth century, and especially during the latter half of the century, fantasy became, in Stephen Prickett’s words, “respectable—for antiquarians, for poets, even for children” (Victorian Fantasy 5), and a genre was born. Many of the classic works of modern fantasy were written during this time, and many of them have become part of our mythology. This course will explore fantasy created during the Victorian period. We will examine fantasy in the form of fairy tales, ghost stories, novels, and poetry. In addition, we will learn about the Victorian period in general. course_title: Early American Literature, Beginnings to Civil War
description: From Spanish colonial encounter narratives, to slave narratives and Lenape oral histories, this course is fundamentally concerned with the way that “America” is a product of cultural encounter. In particular, this course addresses the following skills required for Core Curriculum education: 1. Critical Thinking: creative thinking, innovation, inquiry, and analysis, evaluation and synthesis of information. Students will read a wide variety of authors and perspectives that will challenge them to think critically about what it means to be “American” or write “American literature.” 2. Communication: effective development, interpretation and expression of ideas through written, oral and visual communication. Through in class contributions and a multi-stage essay writing process, students will take their critical observations and fashion them into a structured argument. 3. Social Responsibility: intercultural competence, knowledge of civic responsibility, and the ability to engage effectively in regional, national, and global communities. The ing we call “America” was forged through the clash, conflict and cooperation of different people, ideas and belief systems. Understanding that national culture or national identity is not monolithic, but contested and variable, helps students navigate a globalized world where their perspectives and beliefs are just one of many. 4. Personal Responsibility: ability to connect choices, actions and consequences to ethical decision-making. Class discussions on sensitive topics and historical periods encourage students to understand their own actions and life choices within a wider historical and ethical framework.

What is it? Where is it? Why is it located there? So what? Geography is much more than a collection of facts about capital cities and mountain ranges; the essence of geography is to study why locations and features matter. Geography is the study of spatial organization of human activity, and of people’s relationships with their environment – whether in an urban or a rural setting. How have human activities and social/cultural characteristics in a place been shaped by the landscape? And in turn, how has the landscape been shaped by human activities? This course will introduce you to a variety of concepts and methods that geographers use to analyze spatial patterns and processes. The course is organized regionally, but this does not preclude broader thematic discussions. I hope that this will be an interactive course – and that we can draw on our classmates’ “regions of expertise” to learn from each other. I encourage sharing of any type (articles, literature, music, food…) that will help us “experience” and understand each region.

Sociolinguistics is the empirical study of how society shapes language use and perception (and vice versa). In this course, we will trace the historical development of the field with its three distinctive theoretical waves: • How language is correlated with macro-social factors, such as age, biological sex, social class, country/region of origin (1st wave) • How one’s connections (or lack thereof) with other speech community members impacts language (2nd wave) • How language users perceive social differences through language and how they can utilize the social meaning associated with linguistic forms to project particular identities in specific discursive moments (3rd wave) Drawing from theoretical and empirical sources, as well as our lived experiences as language users, we will apply these concepts to the study of regional and social variation in the Spanish-speaking world. Additionally, this course will exemplify course concepts through the investigation of artistic and non artistic speech of historical and contemporary musicians throughout the Spanish-speaking world.

In 1972, Gloria Steinem famously depicted Wonder Woman on the cover of Ms Magazine, with the headline “Wonder Woman for President” printed across her. Since then, this iconic image of the most famous female superhero has been for many a symbol of the feminist movement. Indeed, Wonder Woman was inspired by the rhetoric of the women’s suffrage movement, and her creator, William Moulton Marston, stated that in creating her character in the 1930s, he wished to empower women. Yet this character is also filled with troubling contradictions. Who exactly is Wonder Woman’s intended audience? What are we to make of the fact that no woman ever received credit for writing or illustrating Wonder Woman comics until the mid 1980s, and no woman was in charge of the series until the early 2000s? How did censorship affect the development and popularity of the character? Is Wonder Woman a different person on film than she is in her comics? This course will study Wonder Woman’s evolution from her creation to the present day and will examine how she mirrors the progress and limitations of the women’s rights movement in America. At the end, students will discuss whether or not Wonder Woman is a good symbol for Women’s and Gender Studies and recommend what they think the iconic heroine should be like.

course_title: Seminar in History of Ideas in the Hispanic World
description: This course is designed to prepare students for academic and professional success in the field of Hispanic Studies as well as in related fields in which they will compete for job placements, such as comparative literature and Caribbean Studies. The course focuses on how ideas have travelled across Latin America and the Caribbean. After reading primary sources from the Hispanic world and the Francophone Caribbean, we will read the work of Sylvia Wynter, a theorist whose training focused on the Hispanic world and who connected that world to Caribbean philosophy. In order to prepare students professionally, course discussions will situate the readings within contemporary scholarly debates taking place in leading journals and professional conferences spaces, such as the Modern Language Association (MLA) and the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA). These debates include vibrant and critical discussions of race, gender, sexuality, colonization, decolonization, civilization, war, peace, development, environmental justice, and many other histories and concepts. These academic spaces are also increasingly interdisciplinary, with scholars making connections across political theory, queer theory, Black Studies, Indigenous Studies, environmental studies, and many other fields. With a knowledge of how several theories and fields intersect, students will have a competitive advantage on the academic job market. The instructor and students may make connections between their experiences and the course readings; this is an accepted research method in the humanities today.

U.S.-Latin America Relations and the Illicit Economy
description: In particular, we will explore the relationship between U.S. security objectives and the illicit economy that has developed in Latin America for the past 50 years. Historically, Latin America has been treated as America’s “backyard.” It was a launch pad for U.S. power projection through the construction of the Panama Canal, was the source of extractive economies for U.S. entrepreneurs as America developed into a global power, and during the Cold War, superpower rivalry in the region, at times, forced a violent backlash against peoples in the region by U.S. leaders. However, the region has not been a strategic priority for the United States in recent decades, and in fact, U.S. policies in Latin America have been dominated by issues relating to the illicit economy, especially the movement of people and goods (i.e., drug trade, the migrant crisis, etc.). This course traces the development of the illicit economy in relation to U.S. security objectives in the region, reflecting on the possibilities for productive relations in the future that decrease militarized policies and promote healthier, more stable societies in the region. To share a hemisphere means sharing everything, the good and bad. The United States and its Latin American partners have played central roles in shaping each other’s economies (licit and illicit) and resulting efforts to police them. We will examine the fundamental tensions between the development of the illicit economy in Latin America—which caters to U.S. demands for labor, goods, and capital—and the prohibitive policies Washington has developed to police the movement of people and goods, and the regions more broadly.

This course entails an exploration and examination of the social determinants and distribution of physical and mental health outcomes. These determinants include socioeconomic inequalities, stress and social organization. The course focuses on the development and evaluation of testable hypotheses concerning the relationship between social conditions and health.

course_title: Foundations of Maternal and Child Health
description: This course provides foundational maternal and child health (MCH) material to: Focus on the determinants, mechanisms and systems that maintain the health, safety, well-being, of children and their families in communities and societies; Describe MCH populations, conceptual frameworks, MCH health indicators and public health programs; Understand major challenges in the MCH field including health disparities, using and applying sound epidemiologic research, research issues, program planning and evaluation; Encourage critical thinking and interdisciplinary collaboration to improve MCH. This course encourages the data-based decision making to improve the health of mothers and children.

This course covers general concepts and techniques of safety upon which more detailed and advanced applications may be based. In addition, concepts will include current system safety analysis techniques, failure mode and effect and fault tree analysis, as well as economic analysis for presentation of alternative solutions for problem solving.

Fundamental topics upon which models for the prevention and control of distal upper extremity disorders are constructed. Focus is on topics including human anatomy, neurophysiology, electrophysiology and worker capacity evaluation

Basic understanding of the theory and practice of human factors particularly as they related to safety domains. Topics are presented within the framework of humans as functioning systems. Specific foci of class are: Analysis (AN) of elements of a work system, i.e., task, human, and environment; application (AP) of Human Factors and Ergonomics (HF/E) analysis to work systems and human machine interfaces; testing (T) & evaluation methods for HF/E scientific efforts and industry domains.

course_title: Health and Safety at Hazardous Waste Sites
description: Course covers OSHA compliance issues related to the protection of personnel engaged in on-site remediation activities. Students who satisfactorily complete the course meet the requirements for initial training under 20 CFR 1910.120 (HAZWOPER) and receive a certificate. Hands-on activities/workshops in the areas of personal protective equipment selection and use, sources of chemical information, decontamination procedures, air monitoring equipment, materials handling, and health and safety planning. Lab fee required.

Identification, evaluation and quantification of risk factors for environmental and occupational diseases, using classic and current examples of exposures involving chemical, physical and biological agents. Selection of appropriate design and groups. Exposure assessment, including biomarkers and molecular dosimetry, genetics, gender, age, socioeconomic and other factors affecting susceptibility. The online section of this course cannot be taken as a repeatable course.

Review of the globalization and transformation of local problems into international issues; environmental problems that developing and underdeveloped countries face due to overpopulation, lack of natural resources, and lack of proper ways or technologies to dispose of hazardous water.

course_title: Texas Training Initiative for Emergency Response
description: This course develops the knowledge, skills, and abilities needed to effectively respond to bioterrorism, infectious disease outbreaks, and other public health threats and emergencies using a multi-disciplinary approach. The course will focus on competencies paralleling the critical benchmark of emergency preparedness as identified by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as well as to gain the knowledge, skills, and abilities along with practice to protect the public's health. The roles of many public health workers will be explored.

This course examines critical topics in U.S. health policy and politics, focusing on legislative processes, political actors, statutory origins, and future implications. Students will analyze policy development, evaluate political influences, and prepare policy briefings (Memos) to enhance decision-making and advocacy skills. This section of PHPM 640 is delivered primarily online as an asynchronous course in Canvas and includes a one-week, in-person Washington, DC immersion focused on federal policymaking, advocacy, and stakeholder engagement.

Globalization of health is evolving dramatically spurred on by the globalization of trade and commerce, migration of peoples, and advances in communication. These changes are having a significant impact on health and health care. Multiple diseases, as influenza, emerging in a local site but then are transmitted at a global or pandemic proportion with a few short weeks or months. International travel and the migration of populations across countries can lead to the introduction of diseases or conditions previously unheard of or noted in only small numbers.

A health system consists of all organizations, people, and actions whose aim is to promote, restore, or maintain health. Like most systems, health systems have defined goals and objectives. However, these systems exist within unique contexts, which can complicate comparative analyses. This course will explore frameworks and approaches for designing and analyzing health systems across the world. Throughout the course, students will be introduced to various international organizations, state actors, and civil society involved in global health systems; assess differing roles and opportunities for public and private actors in health systems; and apply theoretical frameworks for evaluating, designing, and reforming health care systems in different countries.

This course examines how historical planning practices, transportation design, automobile use, and land use policies impact travel behavior and how these policies can both encourage and discourage automobile dependence and the use of alternate transportation modes. Divided into two sections, the course first introduces the concept of sustainable transportation, the current state of U.S. transportation networks, how transportation decisions are made, and concepts such as housing location choice, livability, and policy. The course will then introduce a toolbox of strategies designed to mitigate congestion, promote sustainable transportation goals, and create spaces for healthy living. Students will learn principles, techniques, and examples of sustainable design, non-private auto transportation modes, pricing and parking strategies, active transportation, and traffic management. The latter half of the course will look at emerging trends in transportation like autonomous vehicles and shared mobilities. Students will also learn how truly sustainable transportation must address past planning issues, inequities, and injustices in both historical and contemporary approaches to transportation planning and design.

Exploration of animal welfare issues from an animal's perspective; exploration of the 
general questions that typically affect the welfare of an animal and insight to practices that 
can be used to improve the welfare of an animal.

Exploration of aesthetic, sociocultural, political, and ecological issues in creating art that engages community and affects positive change; study of exemplary artworks and creation of proposals for new ones; emphasis on creative thinking, community involvement, collaborative enterprise, research, and the creation of art works honoring aesthetic and cultural values.

 Review the conservation/environmental history of the United States and how that has influenced current views, laws and regulations related to the environment and land use.  Assess the various approaches to environmental impact assessments.  Understand the content, purpose, and process of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).  Evaluate environmental assessments and environmental impact statements necessary for NEPA compliance.  Determine the permitting process needed to comply with the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and other resource related laws.  Expand awareness of the myriad of laws and regulations that apply to conservation/environmental/land use issues and the professional approach to deal with these often contentious projects.

Study and compare human and natural ecosystems using diversity, interrelations, cycles, and energy as the conceptional organization; central themes of the course are sustainability, stewardship and science. Additional Course Notes Students will learn about and explore how contemporary cultural groups and indigenous people use various physical tools to achieve natural resource management goals, examining the synergy between these goals and societal priorities and expression such as conservation, economic gain, and cultural identity.
Elements of watershed management and principles and practices of wildland management for protection, maintenance and improvement of water resources values; current literature and research advances.

Discussion of physical, chemical, and biological properties of soil and water and the impact on productivity and sustainability of various ecosystems; application of the knowledge of properties and soil processes to develop and evaluate strategies for protecting and/or improving soil and water quality.

course_title: Seminar in Law, Deviance, and Social Control: “Crime, Punishment and the Life Course”
description: This class examines social inequality (e.g., social class, race/ethnicity, gender, age) as correlates of crime, punishment and victimization, and how each of these in turn have consequences for people’s life chances and further social inequality in society. This course facilitates student comprehension and mastery of key concepts, theories and issues in life course criminology. Core concepts include continuity and change in behaviors (i.e., persistence, desistance), revictimization, aging processes, cumulative disadvantage, re-entry from prison into society, and broader life course ideas of trajectories, transitions, and turning points. We focus on guiding life course principles and their development in the context of crime/deviance, victimization, and punishment. Implications of these issues for social policy, theory, and opportunities for prevention and intervention will be considered throughout the course. The course is organized in three parts. In Part I, we examine crime and antisocial behaviors, victimization in Part II, and then criminal legal system contacts and punishment in Part III. In each part, we focus on core principles of life course perspectives. We incorporate both classic and contemporary works to understand the development of the field and current and emerging topics.

course_title: Practice of evaluating human health risks of chemicals
description:
In this course, students will explore how the theory behind all of the major components of human health
risk assessment is applied to real-life challenges and decisions. The main objective is to provide students
with a realistic view of the “big picture” in human health assessment so they would understand how basic
science, public policy and special interests mesh together to produce regulations and/or decisions that
impact public health or the environment. The course will rely extensively on the expertise of the real-life
“practitioners” and afford an opportunity for students to engage in discussions with a diverse set of
stakeholders to further explore their perspectives on the theory and practice of evaluating human health
hazards and risks of chemicals. Real-life examples of how diverse types of information are integrated for
the purpose of judging what chemical exposures may pose a risk to human health.

Advances in the hydrogen economy and hydrogen production from renewable sources; hydrogen
storage, transport, delivery and utilization of clean energy using decarbonization methods; design and
operation of hydrogen production hubs and equipment; integrity of critical maintenance activities; case
studies of commercial applications; current technological challenges and innovations; economic and risk
analyses and their controls.

Examination of economic concepts and tools contributing to the solution of water scarcity problems; development of working knowledge of water resource economics; policy options established and explored; analytical tools for performing policy and project assessment introduced and applied. Prerequisite: MATH 142.

Critical evaluation of policies and procedures in natural resource development and use; identification of problems in resource development, the political-economic decision-making processes and analytical tools which can contribute to economic decisions. Cross Listing: PSAA 663/AGEC 604.
Application of recreation and youth development knowledge to a specific project or program of a cooperating youth development organization.

course_title: Practice and Development of Effective Skills for Youth Development
description: Development of skills and competencies needed to successfully manage paid and volunteer staff, design youth programs, address safety and risk management issues; build community support of public, non-profit, and for profit or commercial youth programs and agencies; history and scope of youth serving organizations; programming and staffing strategies; managing, mentoring and training staff; diverse approaches to program curriculum and design; behavior management and recognition of youth participants; youth protection; relevant laws and legal mandates; safety, health and wellness; youth advocacy and engagement; working with parents and community partners; and issues and innovations in youth development. Prerequisite: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with RPTS 671.

course_title: Practice and Development of Effective Skills for Youth Development
description: Development of skills and competencies needed to successfully manage paid and volunteer staff, design youth programs, address safety and risk management issues; build community support of public, non-profit, and for profit or commercial youth programs and agencies; history and scope of youth serving organizations; programming and staffing strategies; managing, mentoring and training staff; diverse approaches to program curriculum and design; behavior management and recognition of youth participants; youth protection; relevant laws and legal mandates; safety, health and wellness; youth advocacy and engagement; working with parents and community partners; and issues and innovations in youth development. Prerequisite: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with RPTS 671.

course_title: Development and Planning of Community Education Programs
description: Focuses on the principles, theories, techniques, and applications for developing and planning educational program in a community setting; program development strategies, focusing educational programming in relation to issues identified citizens will be developed and enhanced in this course. This course is centered in the fact that communities are the foundation for successful problem solving and management of issues. Through active engagement, we will focus upon principles, theories, techniques, and applications of community building and problem solving which is quintessential to successful extension work and life.

course_title: Food Safety: Policy, Regulations and Issues
description: Designed to explore the complexities of the regulations governing the production of foods of animal origin in the United States; requirements for countries importing products into the United States; federal, state and local requirement will be addressed. Prerequisites: ANSC 457, FSTC 457, ANSC 657, FSTC 657, or approval of instructor.

Explores the paleoecological context in which past humans interacted with the natural environment encompassing plants, animals and landscape. Introduces students to theories and methods relevant to studying past human-environment interactions. Outlines types of environmental data that survive in the archaeological record (geological, botanical, faunal, chemical), recovery and analytical methods, absolute chronology, and inferences made based on these data. Develops long-term, global perspective on human-environment interactions provided by the fields of archaeology and earth science.

course_title: Software Analysis for HVAC Systems in Low Energy Buildings
description: Energy analysis (using EnergyPlus and OpenStudio software) with an emphasis on developing strategies for low energy use. Various heating and cooling systems will be simulated in a low energy building and the impact of the mechanical equipment (including air handling systems, chiller and boilers), the building envelope, energy management control systems and indoor air quality will be analyzed.

Technology behind applied solar energy design, including solar resource evaluation, heat transfer related to solar design, active solar systems, passive solar design, the FCHART and PV FCHART design methods and lifecycle economics.

Students completing ARCH 608 should be able to: ▪ Investigate key issues related to the project, site, and context types. ▪ Demonstrate design thinking skills and develop formal ordering systems in response to the findings of the investigation of the project issues. ▪ Produce the technical documents demonstrating an understanding of the professions responsibility to historical traditions, global culture, accessibility, sustainability, site design, life safety, environmental and structural systems. ▪ Demonstrate initiative, curiosity, discipline, and integrity throughout the design process. ▪ Demonstrate the ability to make design decisions within architectural projects while demonstrating synthesis of user requirements, regulatory requirements, site conditions, and accessible design, and consideration of the measurable environmental impacts of their design decisions in accordance with current NAAB accreditation criteria. (see NAAB section)
