Physical and chemical properties of atmospheric aerosols, including their impact on global climate change, air quality, and human health. Physical principles of particles suspended in air, including rectilinear and curvilinear motion in a force field, diffusion, evaporation, condensation, coagulation, and electrical properties. Aerosol chemical processes including the formation, evolution, and aging of organic aerosols, with an emphasis on fine aerosols.

An advanced survey of fundamental atmospheric processes involving biogeochemical cycles, air 
pollution, tropospheric chemistry, atmospheric aerosols and stratospheric chemistry.

Engineering principles and design of pressurized irrigation systems, introduction to the design of subsurface drainage systems, crop water requirements, soil water properties, irrigation scheduling, sprinkler irrigation, trickle irrigation, irrigation pumps, pipelines, irrigation canals.

This course will introduce students to the advanced concepts of surface and subsurface hydrologic processes, measurements, and modeling techniques across different spatio-temporal scales; contemporary issues related to the soil and water resources, hydrogeology, geochemistry, microbiology, ecology, hydrology, and environmental engineering. The class will be divided into several modules with alternative theory and coding sessions every week. Each module will discuss one component of the hydrologic cycle by introducing its measurement, estimation, and scaling techniques followed by discussions on relevant published literature to aid the students in their final projects. At the end of the course, students will appreciate the issues pertaining to scaling limitations in hydrology and how it impacts our predictions and knowledge of global water cycle.

course_title: Design of Biological Waste Treatment Systems
description: Management and treatment of high organic content wastes, with emphasis on agricultural and food processing wastes; engineering design of biological waste treatment processes; regulatory aspects affecting management of agricultural wastes.

Overview of physical, mechanical, fluid dynamical, electrical, optical, and molecular aspects of bioaerosols; bioaerosol generation, sampling and deposition measurements including size distribution, morphology, chemical composition, bioaerosol samplers, sample analysis, dry and wet deposition, and biofilm resuspension; health effects of bioaerosols, antibiotic resistance, ambient sampling in industrial and agricultural fields.

Introduction to properties and engineering aspects of materials for use as components of a package and/or packaging system; principles of design and development of packages; evaluation of product-package-environment interaction mechanisms; testing methods; environmental concerns; regulations.

course_title: Ethics and Responsible Conduct of Research
description: Instruction on what constitutes fraud in science, how to recognize it and avoid committing fraud; includes basis of ethics and plagiarism; negotiation techniques and conflict management; regulations and ethics covering animal and human experiments; record-keeping; data management; peer review. May be taken four times for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

Foundation in Life Cycle Cost Analysis computation within the context of current issues in environmental sustainability and evidence-based thinking; lean construction as a strategy to overcome the hurdle of first cost.

Fundamentals of smart structures including structural dynamics, damping, sensors, control concepts, smart materials, modeling of smart structures, and signal processing; semi-passive concepts, energy harvesting, semi-active concepts, active vibration control, active noise control, shape adaptation, and structural health monitoring.

Advanced groundwater hydrology, groundwater contamination, groundwater modeling, multiple-phase flow, salt water intrusion, artificial recharge, sustainable groundwater management. Prerequisite: CVEN 462, GEOL 410, or equivalent; or approval of instructor.

course_title: Water Resources Engineering Planning and Management
description: Managing water resources; the planning process, systems analysis methods; institutional framework for water resources engineering; comprehensive integration of engineering, economic, environmental, legal and political considerations in water resources development and management. Prerequisite: Graduate classification in engineering or approval of instructor.

Characterization of air contaminants; health effects and legal aspects; dispersion of pollutants in the atmosphere; technology for the control of gaseous and particulate emissions. Prerequisite: CVEN 311.

The rapid loss of biodiversity is a global crisis with no easy solutions. Slowing the loss requires collaboration, teamwork, and commitment on the part of many, including scholars of different disciplines, practitioners, policy makers, activists, local residents, community leaders, and people in both the private and public sectors, willing to work together. Yet too often, conservationists work in isolation of each other. Universities can be the worst examples of this, with students and professors working in disparate disciplines and departments, not communicating with each other, even as they are focused on the same challenges. Universities can also be the best examples of collaboration, with scholars sharing data, analyses, and insights, and acting together to influence policy and conservation on the ground. The Applied Biodiversity Science (ABS) Program at Texas A&M is one of the positive examples. Created in 2006, ABS is a multidisciplinary community of scholars focused on biodiversity loss and conservation. This graduate course is a foundation of ABS, introducing students to some of the main paradigms guiding conservation science. Co-taught by a conservation biologist and an environmental anthropologist, the seminar is a platform for dialogue and collaboration.

course_title: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for Resource Management
description: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) approach to solving spatial problems and managing natural resources, including the acquisition, management, manipulation, analysis, and mapping of spatial and non-spatial databases; identification of natural and relevant features from various data sources; integration of relevant technologies and data; extensive use of GIS software to solve real-world problems.

This course provides a framework for understanding how plants and animals affect the water cycle. We examine and explore the water cycle in all of its aspects with the idea of understanding how changes in land cover may influence the water cycle; implications for both upland and riparian systems.

Philosophical basis, theoretical framework, and practical application of systems analysis and simulation within the context of ecology and natural resource management; emphasis placed on development, evaluation, and use of simulation models by students.

course_title: Smart Power Distribution Systems Analysis and Operation
description: Study of element models in active power distribution systems in smart grid operation from a physics and engineering perspective; exploration of emerging topics such as integrating solar panels, microgrid operations, advanced metering infrastructure, and restoration and outage management for active power distribution systems; and exposure to software tools for solving three-phase unbalanced power flow analysis and simple distribution system optimal power flow problems.

Overview of high voltage direct current (HVDC) power transmission technology. This includes the motivations for HVDC, power grid system level operation, HVDC power electronics and controls and real world example installations of HVDC systems. Graduate standing in electrical engineering and background in power systems is required. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to: 
• Understand fundamentals of HVDC technology. 
• Understand basic power electronics for HVDC.  
• Specify and design basic building blocks of HVDC.  
• Understand motivations and applications of HVDC power in the power gird.  
• Understand the technical benefits of HVDC systems in sustainable power generation systems.

• Understand the cost of higher education and implications on college affordability and accessibility, as well as national, state, and local funding policy. • Examine models of higher education budgeting and resource allocation within the framework of institutional types (public/private, Carnegie classification, etc.). • Describe the fiduciary policy role of federal and state governing bodies, including executive and legislative branches, governing boards, accreditation agencies, etc. • Critically apply research, scholarship, and theory to higher education business applications. • Describe higher education as a public and/or private good relative to past, current, and future policy.

course_title: Historical Analysis of Urban School Reform
description: In EDCI 629, students will be able to: • Analyze, synthesize and lead discussions on current educational topics affecting urban schools and communities • Examine neighborhoods, communities, and schools as contexts for teaching and learning opportunities. • Discuss how benchmarks have influenced and shaped urban education in American schools, past and present. • Describe and analyze specific benchmarks that impact(ed) urban education related to acts, trends, programs, legal mandates and laws. • Explore, analyze and discuss benchmarks related to domestic interests, globalization, finance, and demographics • Be able to discuss research and urban education. • Write a research-based paper on a specific benchmark in urban education.

course_title: Topics in Gender, Literature, and Culture: Women Writing Nature
description: “Women Writing Nature” is designed as a survey of women’s representations of human interactions with the more-than-human world from the late 18th century to the present. The course will feature essays, memoirs, poetry, theory and novels from a range of women writers, including biologists, creative writers, anthropologists, philosophers, botanists, activists and travelers (in many cases, these categories will overlap in a single being). The historical breadth will allow us to track approaches to the natural world across two and a half centuries. For instance, when the Scottish traveler and amateur botanist Maria Calcott Graham visited Chile in 1824, she was both an agent of the British incursion in South America and an early proponent of Traditional Ecological/Indigenous Knowledge, learning many plant names and their uses from native Chileans. Like the Potawatomi botanist Robin Wall Kimmerer, Graham valued indigenous knowledge alongside her understanding of Linnaean botany. Similarly, discussions of human cultivation of the natural world could run through Andrea Wulf’s work on the gardens of the revolutionary period that shaped American national identity, to Louisa May Alcott’s Transcendental Wild Oats, Charlotte Perkins Gilman’s Herland, Becky Chamber’s futuristic Psalm for the Wild-Built and Camille Dungy’s Soil. The potential readings below and additional critical articles will give us a wide ranging foundation in ecofeminism, animism, environmental justice, decolonial trajectories, and the stakes of our own entanglements with the natural world.

Introduction to the fundamentals of biomass (biochemistry and resources); basics of important processing technologies for the pre-treatment and conversion of biomass to useful products. Prerequisite: Graduate classification; ENGY majors.

course_title: Vector-Borne Disease Management and Response in Human and Animal Systems
description: Integration of arthropod vector biology and surveillance with response and management of vector-borne disease outbreaks; complex interactions of diverse authorities in vector-borne disease management and response; participation in designing, operating, and assessing outbreak response and management plans; capstone experience in the Vector Biology and Vector-Borne Disease Response Certificate.

course_title: Social and Emotional Development and Interventions
description: School systems, educators and researchers are increasingly recognizing the fundamental role that children’s social and emotional skills play in in their scholastic and meet academic success. Beyond educational outcomes, children’s social and emotional competencies are integral to the development of well-rounded students who can contribute to civic society. Consequently, there have been a plethora of school-based social and emotional learning (SEL) programs that have been implemented across the U.S. and internationally. Although many of these programs are evidence based and appear to be promising, there has been considerable variability across programs in their goals, program designs and outcomes. This course has two primary aims: 1) To explore the theoretical foundations of social and emotional development from early childhood through adolescence. 2) To review the current state of SEL intervention programs.

History, development of, and fundamental principles behind current food regulations, including food labeling, adulteration, food safety, food additives, dietary supplements, and import and export laws; overview of government agency jurisdiction, international law and ethics.

This course will cover the basic principles and techniques of food biomanufacturing, including bioprocessing, fermentation science, cellular agriculture, space food, and molecular farming, by addressing bioprocessing, microbial community, bacterial and yeast-based fermentation, bioreactors, cellular agriculture technologies, enzymes applications in food production, and sustainability. Students will be introduced to the concepts of cellular agriculture, fermentation and precision fermentation, bioprocessing, different bioreactors, and life cycle analysis roles in making decisions about the final products. Also, students will learn about how to read papers to develop protocols and how to modify them. The course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of upstream and downstream processing, which will cover the bacterial and yeast-based fermentation, precision fermentation, cellular agriculture, bioprocessing, and food safety aspects of these products. The course will include at least two lectures from other researchers and scientists from industry and other institutions. The course will also cover biomanufacturing applications for different products developed from plants, insects, algae, and animals’ byproducts.

Chemistry of aqueous solutions; weathering/redox reactions and controls on fresh waters; natural and anthropogenic factors affecting major, minor, and trace elements in fresh waters; evaluation of fresh water composition; application of water-quality measurements to quantitative hydrology. Cross-listed with WMHS 640

course_title: Special Topics: Mixed Methods Research and Evaluation in Public Health
description: Introduction to mixed methods research and evaluation in the public health sciences and the social and behavioral health sciences, with particular focus on mixed methods designs, mixed method analytical techniques, and mixed method writing and publishing in the public health field.

course_title: Community Organization and Assessment – HBEH 610 – section 600
description: Integration of knowledge and skills gained through other courses and experiences at SPH allowing an understanding of both the overall public health problem-solving approach and the contributions of each discipline to that approach; working in groups to analyze public health problems and develop interventions. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. This course examines the nature of community and its role as setting, target and facilitator of health among its population. Topics include approaches to assessing community factors that influence health status, particularly the social determinants of health, and application of that information in planning community-based interventions.

Identification and use of indigenous and introduced landscape plants; plants for special uses in urban environments; emphasis on plants' ornamental attributes, cultural requirements, and adaptability in urban and suburban environments. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: HORT 308 or HORT 609. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Continuation (Part II) of development of a research project under the guidance of the instructor and other team members as applicable; construction of a data analysis, solutions, ROI; mid-term steering committee meeting, final report and presentation towards completion of final capstone project. Prerequisites: Enrollment in the Master of Industrial Distribution program.

The course will begin with demographics as the people-based underpinning of the other two themes. The demographics focus will include an accounting of African demographic growth and a focus on estimates that project Africa to account for the majority of the globe’s population growth this century, and that the continent by 2100 will account for 40 percent of the world’s population. We will grapple with the population forecasts of countries such as Nigeria, projected to double from just over 200 million today to 400 million by 2050, surpassing the United States as the third most populous country in the world. We will wrestle with what demographic trends mean for conflict and development and whether African states will reap a demographic dividend or suffer the plight of population overload. We will examine how demographic trends affect international security. The focus on conflict will include key drivers and responses. Class exercises will dive into the experience of national security practitioners and how they navigate conflict on the continent and from third countries and international organizations. We will debate whether the continent is stuck in a cycle of conflict or moving toward a more peaceful future. Our focus on development will move beyond the theoretical and draw on our lessons from demographics and conflict to examine practitioners' experiences today and possibilities for the future, especially as the development landscape undergoes an unprecedented overhaul. Like our focus on conflict, our exercises will dive into the experience of national security practitioners and how they navigate development openings and obstacles.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 changed dramatically the European security landscape. This course examines key developments and challenges to contemporary European security order. It focuses on issues confronting the European Union: Russia’s war on Ukraine and its implications, post-Brexit Britain and its role, China’s increasing influence, and other critical security challenges. We will further analyze and build upon the first lessons learned from the security challenges and vulnerabilities of the transatlantic security architecture exposed by Russia’s war on Ukraine. Finally, we will examine the emerging contours of the new postwar European security order and its implications for transatlantic and global security. Students will be able to hone their analytical, writing, and presentation skills; develop a multidisciplinary approach to analyzing the problems discussed, and develop the skills of theorizing, formulating hypotheses, and justifying their views about the course topics. The practical coursework will be based on interactive learning techniques and will comprise individual and group presentations, and written assignments.

course_title: Clientelism & Corruption in the Developing World
description: This course will critically examine various approaches to the study of clientelism in developing countries, with a particular focus on political institutions and party politics. Students will learn the meaning of clientelism, how it relates to corruption, electoral fraud, and patrimonialism, and how clientelist practices such as vote buying, and patronage are still being practiced in many developing societies. We will investigate the causes of this phenomenon, the factors for its prevalence in the 21st century and its implications for the quality of democracy.

This course offers a comprehensive exploration of Latin America’s developmental trajectory over the past two centuries, emphasizing historical processes, international contexts, and internal dynamics. Through a critical analysis of key economic, social, and political changes, students will examine how Latin America “fell behind” the United States and the world’s economic leaders, and the complex reasons underlying its relative backwardness. The course emphasizes the region’s multifaceted history of growth, instability, policy experimentation, and inequality. Students will study patterns of population and GDP growth, improvements in life expectancy and education, and significant reductions in poverty—while also interrogating the persistent volatility brought about by changing international terms of trade and financial flows. Critical topics include: The role of international influences—especially the contemporary impact of rising powers such as China. Cyclical booms and busts, and their impact on long-term development. Shifts in development models in response to evolving ideologies, global events, and domestic pressures. The enduring challenge of inequality—within countries, between countries, and in comparison to global leaders. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to discuss the diversity of development experiences in Latin America, understand the ongoing processes shaping the region’s place in the world economy, and critically assess prospects for closing gaps in income, opportunity, and living standards

This is a graduate course that provides theoretical and empirical aspects of the role, potential and limitations of major International Organizations (IO) in world politics. IOs play an important role in efforts to resolve a wide range of universal problems, particularly peace and security, human rights, poverty, and other related matters of concern to international society. The bulk of the course is devoted to an in-depth examination of the United Nations agencies as well as a selected number of international organizations. Questions include: What is the role and record of the IOs in managing conflicts, alleviating poverty, protecting human rights violations, preserving environmental standards and prosecuting international criminals?

The course will review various definitions of development and the theories which explain why some countries develop and others do not. Current controversies will be examined about what factors lead to economic growth; what role good governance and democratic institutions, the cultural values of a society, and social services play in development. Finally, the course will analyze how the foreign aid programs of donor governments and international institutions affect the development process, the politics of aid programs and the mechanisms for their implementation, and the role of new actors in development such as non-governmental organizations, corporations, and foundations.

In today’s rapidly changing global economy, nations are more interconnected than ever before. Thanks to technological advances in transport and communication, goods, services, and money flow easily across borders. This close-knit economic integration offers exciting opportunities but also comes with its own set of complex challenges. On the bright side, international trade encourages cooperation between countries, gives consumers more choices, and boosts the profits of businesses, opening up a world of possibilities for companies in the international market. However, the surge in globalization also creates a multitude of new contenders, making competition both broader and fiercer. The gains from globalization are not shared equally either; while some benefit greatly, others may face significant obstacles. Furthermore, closely related economies introduce new complexities for foreign policy, economic management, and consumer decisions. This course is structured into three main modules, each designed to help you make sense of the global economic landscape and develop the tools to navigate it successfully: This course aims to equip students with the intellectual tools to understand our global economic environment. The course has three main components that cover the basics of international economics: 1. Trade and Policies: Study the mechanics of international trade and trade policies. Explore the concept of comparative advantage and its implications, understand the characteristics of tariff and non-tariff barriers, and analyze the strategies countries employ to navigate the competitive global marketplace. 2. International Finance: Gain insight into the balance of payments and understand the workings of foreign exchange markets. Grasp the forces that influence exchange rates, study the dynamics of capital flows, and uncover the interplay between financial globalization and economic stability. 3. Global Challenges: Navigate the current global challenges between economics and international relations. Explore the symbiotic relationship between economic growth, foreign aid, and environmental sustainability.

This course will focus on post-disaster recovery. Topics that will be addressed include conceptualizations of recovery and restoration at multiple levels of analysis including household, business, and community. While various forms of hazards or potential disasters will be discussed the primary focus will be on natural, environmental, and technological hazards. This course emphasizes the necessary connection between recovery, preparation, response, and mitigation; because, without an integrated approach, recovery processes can be delayed and, even more importantly, recovery can and often does set the seeds for future disasters. Indeed, when considering what is meant by resilience – bouncing back, but bouncing back such that the system is more adapted -- then, recovery as part of an integrated set of strategies is critical for resilience. So, in some sense, this course is all about resilience with a focus on recovery processes and strategies.

course_title: Special Topics in Health Law and Policy
description: This interprofessional course taught jointly at the School of Law and the Bush School of Government and Public Service covers fundamental issues in health law and policy from both legal and public policymaking perspectives. Health care represents approximately one-sixth of the American economy, as skilled personnel provide life-saving services using advanced technology. It also gives rise to important and controversial challenges at the individual, community, and population levels, which the course unpacks and discusses. Although some continue to regard the U.S. health care system as “the best in the world,” the COVID-19 pandemic has revealed major shortcomings not only in the nation’s public health preparedness, but also in the fairness and efficiency of American medical care. Nor is the direction of national health policy Page 1 of 10 Course Syllabus clear. Enacted in 2010, a full century after universal health coverage was first proposed in the United States, the Affordable Care Act (aka “Obamacare”) has intensified public policy debate rather than resolving it. Recent executive, legislative, and judicial actions have cast further uncertainty on the goals and outcomes of the Affordable Care Act, on public health activities, and on biomedical innovation. Recent developments take place against a complex set of federal and state health laws and regulations, other laws governing matters such as complex business practices and risks of injury to persons, and health professional self-regulation and ethics. Framing a set of deceptively simple questions, the class explores many of the core challenges in health system design, operation, and governance. Which countries have the best health care systems, and why? What roles should government play in health care, and what roles should it avoid? Does the U.S. make too many social problems into medical ones, or too few? What is the best way to support the cost of care for those who are too sick or too poor to afford it themselves? How can we spend less on health care and get more for our money? To what degree should the future health care system be controlled by physicians? How can individuals and communities become healthier? What policy and system-level interventions are most effective for reducing preventable gaps in health outcomes across communities? What policies would most effectively further innovation? Finally, how has law defined these problems and how can legal change facilitate their solution?

its focus on the population-level, and not the individual-level. Epidemiological principles guide
